paper_sections.title: History of withdrawal modulates drug- and food-cue reactivity in cocaine dependent participants
Neural reactivity to DRUG and FOOD videos
Moderating role of drug use history and psychopathic traits

description.value: The study reassessed an existing cocaine-dependent and non-dependent sample to determine whether a history of DSM-assessed cocaine withdrawal modulates neural reactivity biases toward drug-related versus food-related reward cues, and whether drug-use history and psychopathic traits further influence those biases.

design.value: Secondary analyses of an existing sample compared drug- and food-cue reactivity among cocaine-dependent participants with a history of withdrawal (WD), cocaine-dependent participants without a history of withdrawal (N-WD), and non-dependent participants (ND). Exploratory hierarchical regression analyses evaluated moderation by major drug use history and psychopathic traits.

name.value: Structured Clinical Interview for DSM Disorders (SCID-IV)

description.value: Administered by trained MA-level research staff to assess all psychiatric disorders, including the presence of lifetime cocaine dependence disorder.

Participants were asked whether they had ever experienced withdrawal symptoms after cutting down or stopping cocaine and whether they had used cocaine or another drug to prevent withdrawal symptoms. Participants answering yes were assessed for dysphoric mood and at least two withdrawal symptoms occurring within a few hours to several days following cessation.

task_description.value: Participants performed a cue-reactivity paradigm during which they viewed two identical runs of 29 videos. Fifteen videos depicted individuals preparing or using cocaine and 14 depicted individuals preparing or eating food. Videos were separated by an inter-trial jitter of either 2000, 3500, or 5000 ms to aid deconvolution from the standard hemodynamic response function.

stimuli.value: Video clips related to the creation/administration of either drugs or food: preparing or using cocaine through various means [snorting, injecting], and preparing or eating various foods [hamburger, sandwich].

description.value: Participants performed the cue-reactivity paradigm within a 3T Siemens TrioTim MRI scanner. Two identical runs were acquired, with 29 videos per run; videos lasted approximately 10,000–14,000 ms and were separated by 2000, 3500, or 5000 ms inter-trial jitters.

model_settings.value: The hemodynamic response during presentation of FOOD and DRUG videos was modeled, with six movement parameters (x, y, z, pitch, yaw, roll) included in the first-level design matrix.

The model included Group (WD, N-WD, ND), VideoType (DRUG, FOOD), and the Group*VideoType interaction. Whole-brain results were threshold at 0.001 uncorrected with an extended cluster threshold of 102 voxels, equivalent to p < .05 FWE. Small-volume corrected search spheres were 10 mm for cortical regions and 6 mm for subcortical regions.

Among dependent participants, Group (WD or N-WD), PCL-R scores, and MDU scores were entered as separate first-level regressors; Group * PCL-R, Group * MDU, and PCL-R * MDU interaction terms were entered as second-level regressors; and the three-way interaction term was entered as a third-level regressor. Models were run both with and without age included in the model. Reported results did not include age as a covariate.
